title: The Skills Required Before Accountability
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that holding team members accountable for outcomes only works if two underlying, often-overlooked skills are already in place, keeping small commitments to colleagues, and consistently following up on tasks. The author distinguishes genuine integrity failures from the much more common problem of distraction and forgetfulness around small promises. Follow-up gets similar treatment, the piece notes many capable team members simply haven't developed the habit. The overall claim is that accountability systems fail because these two foundational skills were never explicitly taught or coached.
points: Holding people accountable for outcomes only works if two foundational, often-overlooked skills already exist, keeping small commitments and consistently following up.
Most failures to keep small promises stem from distraction and forgetfulness, not genuine integrity problems.
The habit of following up and proactively giving status updates is described as underdeveloped in many capable team members.
The piece's central claim is that accountability systems often fail because these two foundational skills were never explicitly taught.
quotes: Often overlooked, however, are two essential skills that enable team members to become accountable in the first place: the ability to keep commitments to colleagues, and the dedication to follow up on everyday tasks and activities.
It is much more common for colleagues to become distracted and forgetful about the small commitments they have made to others.
In too many instances, they are left high and dry by a colleague who has not completed a task they are depending on to finish their work.
Leaders who demonstrate this skill through their example help others see the importance of follow-up, but it is not enough.
Laying the skillful foundations for accountability is essential work. Effective leadership is often created brick by brick.
